title: Tony Chocolonely
subtitle: Ethical sourcing model versus financial and operational challenges.

Making ethical sourcing manageable

This project uses Tony’s Chocolonely’s cocoa sourcing model to examine how traceability, long-term partnerships, and stronger farmer cooperatives address poverty, child- and forced-labor risks, and environmental pressures. It asks how ethical sourcing can scale while remaining operationally and financially viable.

Connecting sourcing principles to structural causes

The analysis considers farmer poverty, unequal market power, weak institutions, and the limits of certification. It focuses on three sourcing principles: supporting a living income, maintaining long-term partnerships, and strengthening cooperatives.

These principles address income pressure, uncertainty, premium distribution, governance, and productive capacity. The project therefore looks beyond certification to whether farmers can participate in a viable supply system over time.

Measuring social, environmental, and economic performance

Proposed measures include living-income progress, child-labor monitoring and remediation system (CLMRS) detection and remediation, cooperative capacity, deforestation and land use, resource efficiency, and carbon footprint per ton of cocoa.

Economic measures include profitability, cost-effectiveness, Open Chain partner growth, and market performance. Recommendations cover collaborative scaling, certification reform and NGO partnerships, traceability technology, and climate resilience.

Why the project matters

Credible ethical sourcing requires purchasing relationships, income measures, and remediation mechanisms that can be followed over time. The project connects social objectives to supply continuity, cost, and scale, treating responsible sourcing as part of long-term supply-chain design.

This article presents the analysis and recommendations from a course project.
